candidates.title: Context-Aware Memorization Detection via Adversarial Compression for Copyright Compliance
candidates.summary: This paper proposes a method to detect verbatim memorization in language models by applying adversarial compression ratio (ACR) metrics, which identify training data reconstructable from shorter prompts. The approach uses probabilistic extraction to quantify memorization risks, evaluated on deduplicated datasets and compared against baselines. It aims to provide a practical tool for assessing copyright violations by identifying memorized content.
candidates.gap: Existing probabilistic extraction methods (ref-029) quantify extraction likelihood but do not measure the compression ratio between prompt length and reconstructed text length, leaving a gap in assessing how efficiently training data can be reconstructed from minimal prompts. Ref-009 defines ACR but does not integrate probabilistic sampling or deduplication.
candidates.approach: The approach computes ACR (ref-009) by finding the shortest prompt that reconstructs a target sequence with high probability. It uses probabilistic extraction (ref-029) to measure reconstruction likelihood across multiple queries, applied to deduplicated datasets (ref-011). The core mechanism differs from ref-009 by incorporating probabilistic sampling and from ref-029 by optimizing for minimal prompt length. Inputs: a model, a target sequence, and a deduplicated dataset. Output: ACR score and reconstruction probability. Objective: minimize prompt length while maximizing reconstruction probability.
candidates.evaluation: The method is evaluated on the deduplicated C4 subset (ref-011) against baselines: discoverable extraction (greedy sampling, ref-050) and probabilistic extraction (ref-029). Metrics include ACR scores, reconstruction probabilities, and exact matches to copyrighted books (ref-044). Ablation studies compare ACR alone, probabilistic extraction alone, and their combination. Legal compliance is tested by checking if exact matches to copyrighted works exist in the model's memorized content.

candidates.title: Hybrid Alignment via Constitutional Classifiers and Human Feedback for Jailbreak Resistance
candidates.summary: This paper proposes a hybrid alignment method combining constitutional classifiers (trained on synthetic data from natural language rules) with human feedback fine-tuning. The approach aims to defend against universal and many-shot jailbreaks while maintaining deployment viability through ablation studies isolating each component's contribution.
candidates.gap: While constitutional classifiers (ref-004) defend against universal jailbreaks, they fail against many-shot attacks (ref-038). Human feedback fine-tuning (ref-016) improves alignment but does not explicitly address jailbreak robustness. No prior work combines both to test if their hybrid mitigates both attack types.
candidates.approach: The method trains constitutional classifiers on synthetic data generated by LLMs using natural language rules (a 'constitution') to filter harmful outputs. These classifiers are integrated with human feedback fine-tuning (ref-016, ref-025) via a two-stage pipeline: (1) classifier filters outputs during supervised fine-tuning, (2) filtered outputs are ranked by human preferences. The hybrid differs from ref-004 by adding human feedback and from ref-016 by incorporating classifier-based filtering. Inputs: model outputs; outputs: filtered and preference-ranked responses; objective: minimize harmful content while preserving helpfulness.
candidates.evaluation: The method is evaluated on (1) ref-038's many-shot jailbreak dataset and (2) ref-014's automated jailbreak suffixes. Baselines include (a) constitutional classifiers alone (ref-004), (b) human feedback alone (ref-016), and (c) unaligned models. Metrics: (1) jailbreak success rate (binary: harmful content generated), (2) refusal rate (proportion of queries rejected), (3) inference overhead. Ablation studies compare hybrid vs. individual components on both attack types.

candidates.title: Deduplication Reduces Verbatim Memorization of Copyrighted Texts in LLMs
candidates.summary: This paper quantifies how training data deduplication reduces verbatim memorization of copyrighted texts in LLMs. By removing near-duplicate sequences, the approach decreases the probability of exact reproductions during generation. The method is evaluated on literary datasets (e.g., books) using extraction attacks, with baselines including undeduplicated models and controlled ablations.
candidates.gap: While ref-011 and ref-044 show deduplication reduces memorization, their analyses do not isolate deduplication's effect on copyrighted material. Ref-011 measures general memorization reduction, and ref-044 quantifies memorization in undeduplicated models but does not test deduplication's impact. The specific effect of deduplication on copyrighted text memorization remains unquantified.
candidates.approach: Apply ref-011's deduplication tools to a dataset of copyrighted books (e.g., ref-044's 200-book subset). Train models on (1) undeduplicated data, (2) deduplicated data, and (3) data with only non-copyrighted duplicates removed. Use ref-050's extraction attacks to measure verbatim memorization rates, defined as the probability of generating a 10+ token exact match to a training example. The core difference from ref-011 is the focus on copyrighted content and controlled ablations.
candidates.evaluation: Measure verbatim memorization rates on the 200-book dataset (ref-044) for models trained on the three data variants. Baselines include undeduplicated models (ref-044) and models trained on data with only non-copyrighted duplicates removed. The ablation isolates deduplication's effect by comparing (1) vs. (2) and (3) vs. (2). Metrics include exact-match extraction rates and the number of extractable books. No legal risk modeling is performed, as no reference links extraction rates to legal outcomes.
